flags: minor: the error in the same series (item 02, 'wiping') is visible while solving 01; students still easily keep 'opened' parallel with 'reached'
E029-01.notes: Past-tense series opened / reached / wiped; B (present perfect), C (conditional perfect), D (participle) all break parallelism with 'reached'.

E029-02.notes: Third verb in series must match 'opened' and 'reached'; 'had wiped' shifts tense, 'wipes' is present, 'wiping' is a fragment element.

E029-03.notes: Following noun phrase is not an independent clause, so semicolon fails; colon introduces the explanation of 'a solution'. Comma (B) makes 'a rubber blade...' read ambiguously as an appositive to 'home'; D runs together. Facts check out: 1902 NYC streetcar trip, 1903 patent, Canadian firm rejection, patent expired 1920.

E029-04.notes: Prior sentence says blade was connected to a lever but not how the lever moved it; the addition clarifies the mechanism, so B's 'repeats' is false. A and C misdescribe the sentence.

E029-05.notes: One 'Canadian firm' (and later 'its engineers') requires singular possessive firm's.

E029-06.notes: Nonrestrictive clause 'which arrived some weeks later' opened by a comma must be closed by a comma before 'was'. C misplaces the comma; D semicolon splits subject from verb.

flags: minor: answer cue - key is the shortest option and A/B are obviously wordy; C (then/than) is the only real distractor
E029-07.notes: Concise and correct; C uses 'then' for comparison; A and B are redundant.

E029-08.notes: Contrast: patent earned nothing, yet by the time it expired wipers were becoming common. 'Therefore' implies false causation; 'for example' and 'similarly' don't fit.

E029-09.notes: Plural subject 'few drivers' takes 'know'; present tense matches 'Today it is hard...'.

E029-10.notes: Essay traces invention to snowy streetcar observation. B cites electric wipers never mentioned; C overstates one paragraph; D irrelevant.
